    (void)TrainFeaturizer(c, batch, opt, /*unit_norm_decoder=*/false);   // decoder norms carry the result
}

std::vector<CrosscoderLatentStats> stats = CrosscoderLatents(c);   // per feature: norms, Δnorm, cosine
LatentClass cls = ClassifyLatent(stats[i]);                        // AOnly, BOnly, Shared, Other
// candidates: the feature indices to test, for example those with Δnorm above 0.9.
std::vector<LatentScaling> ls = MeasureLatentScaling(c, held_out, candidates);   // ν per feature
std::vector<double> ev = ExplainedVarianceBySource(c, held_out);

With sources > 2 and one model's layers side by side, the same class finds features that span several layers.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
The API calls features latents, as the papers do. Source a is source 0 (the base model) and b is source 1 (the fine-tune); swap the source arguments to ask the other way round.

Decoder norms. - Δnorm (Minder et al.) is ½ (1 + (‖d_b‖ − ‖d_a‖) / max(‖d_a‖, ‖d_b‖)). It is 0 for a feature only in model a, 1 for one only in model b, and ½ for an even split. relative_norm, ‖d_b‖ / (‖d_a‖ + ‖d_b‖), agrees at those three points. - ClassifyLatent uses Minder et al.'s bins: below 0.1 a-only, above 0.9 b-only, 0.4 to 0.6 shared, and other in between (0.1 to 0.4, 0.6 to 0.9). - The cosine between a shared feature's two decoders says whether both models write it in the same direction.

Latent Scaling. Decoder norms can mislead: a feature can look one-model when it isn't, and the other way round. Latent Scaling (Minder et al.) checks each candidate against the data. For each model it fits a scale β: how much of the feature's b-side direction, times its code, best explains that model's activations. ν = β_a / β_b is then how much model a uses the feature, relative to model b. Near 0 means model a doesn't need it; near 1 means both do.

It is fitted against two targets: - ν_error: against what the other features leave unexplained in each model. A high value means complete shrinkage: model a needs the feature too, but its a-side decoder was shrunk to almost nothing. - ν_reconstruction: against the crosscoder's reconstruction. A high value means latent decoupling: other features write the same thing into model a.

A feature is specific to model b when ν_reconstruction < 0.5 and ν_error < 0.2.

Run Latent Scaling, not only the bins. In both experiments below, the bins missed what Latent Scaling found.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: Variant Option How it differs L1 (Lindsey et al.) o.sparsity = CrosscoderSparsity::L1 Penalty λ Σ_i f_i Σ_s ‖d_i^s‖: a sum of decoder norms, so a one-model feature stays cheap BatchTopK (Minder et al.) the default The batch's N·k largest f_i Σ_s ‖d_i^s‖ are kept; codes aren't shrunk; a threshold at inference Delta-Crosscoder (Kassem et al.) o.delta = true Separate shared and "delta" feature sets, each with its own top-k; a loss that makes the delta features alone predict x_fine-tune − x_base. Meant for narrow fine-tunes

docs.title: What we found
docs.text:
Planted features (tests/crosscoder_test.cpp). Two synthetic "models" share 16 features, and each has 4 of its own. - When every feature is common (8% of inputs), BatchTopK recovers all 24 and puts each in the right class. - In a narrow fine-tune, the fine-tune adds 4 rare features (0.5% of inputs each). - The crosscoder learns them, but the bins call none of them fine-tune-only (mean Δnorm 0.76). Their base-model decoders keep about half their norm, even after 10 times more training. - Latent Scaling calls all 4 fine-tune-specific, and all 16 shared ones needed by both models. - The Delta-Crosscoder doesn't fix the norms. Its top-k must keep N·k delta activations per batch even when the fine-tune's features are rarer than that.

SmolLM2-135M against SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, with the command above (--crosscoder btk, l1 --l1 5e-4 or delta; 12 epochs at a learning rate of 1e-3 each): 504K tokens, layer 15 of 30, 4,608 features, scored on 50K held-out tokens. The Delta-Crosscoder used its defaults, 32 active delta features and 64 shared.

BatchTopK (k = 32) L1 (λ = 5e-4) Delta-Crosscoder Explained variance (both models) 0.93 0.93 0.96 L0 32 46 96 One-model features by the bins 0 11 0 Instruct-specific by Latent Scaling, of the 50 leaning furthest 8 1 12 Share of those features' activation on chat-template tokens (which are 22% of all tokens) 86% 99% 84%
  • What chat tuning added is about the chat template. The Instruct-specific features fire on <|im_start|>, the role name, and the newline that closes a turn's header. Minder et al. found the same in Gemma 2.
  • The bins alone find almost nothing for two models this close. Latent Scaling is what separates the specific features.
  • The Delta-Crosscoder finds the most, but at three times the L0, which also explains its higher explained variance.

These are small runs: Minder et al. train on 100M tokens.

docs.title: How it's checked
docs.text:
All three variants match a PyTorch rendering (tools/golden/make_crosscoder_golden.py) through the loss, every gradient and two Adam steps.

Conventions: - The loss is the mean squared error over every source plus the penalty, on the same scale as the other featurizers; Lindsey et al. sum it. - Every feature starts with the same decoder in every source, at norm 0.05 for L1 and 1 for BatchTopK (Minder et al.'s values). - The Delta-Crosscoder paper has no public code, so it follows the paper's equations. Its separate sparsity term is left out, since the top-k already fixes the sparsity.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Lindsey et al., "Sparse Crosscoders for Cross-Layer Features and Model Diffing", Transformer Circuits, 2024.
  • Minder, Dumas et al., "Overcoming Sparsity Artifacts in Crosscoders to Interpret Chat-Tuning", arXiv 2504.02922.
  • Kassem et al., "Delta-Crosscoder: Robust Crosscoder Model Diffing in Narrow Fine-Tuning Regimes", arXiv 2603.04426.

docs.title: Parameter Decomposition
docs.text:
Featurizers explain a network's activations. Parameter decomposition explains its weights. The idea: a weight matrix does several separate jobs at once. Split it into pieces so that every input needs only a few pieces to get the same output. Each piece is then one part of the network's mechanism, and you can ask which inputs use which pieces.

pulsatrix implements two methods from Goodfire's line of work: - SPD, stochastic parameter decomposition (Bushnaq, Braun and Sharkey); - VPD, adversarial parameter decomposition (Bushnaq et al., 2026), its successor. Goodfire names it "VPD" for adVersarial Parameter Decomposition. It isn't a variational method.

docs.title: The idea in three terms
docs.text:
• Subcomponents. Each weight matrix W is written as a sum of C rank-one pieces: W ≈ Σ_c V[:, c] U[c, :], or W ≈ V U. Training asks the pieces to add back up to W, a loss called faithfulness.
  • Causal importance. A small network gives each subcomponent a score g in [0, 1] for each input: how much that input needs it.
  • Stochastic masks. Training scales each subcomponent by a random mask m = g + (1 − g) r, with r uniform in [0, 1]. An important subcomponent (g near 1) is kept whole. An unimportant one is scaled randomly, and the output must not change. So g can only stay low for subcomponents an input really doesn't use.

A penalty on g (importance minimality) pushes each input to use as few subcomponents as possible. After training, a subcomponent is a mechanism, and g says which inputs use it.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Wrap each LinearModule you want to decompose in a ComponentLinear, and build the model from the wrappers. This works for models assembled from layers you hold yourself, in containers like SequentialModule and ResidualModule that keep pointers to them.

#include "pulsatrix/adam_optimizer.hpp"
#include "pulsatrix/parameter_decomposition.hpp"
#include "pulsatrix/relu_module.hpp"
#include "pulsatrix/sequential_module.hpp"

// The trained target: w1 (5 → 2), w2 (2 → 5), then a ReLU.
ComponentLinear c1(w1, /*components=*/20, &backend), c2(w2, 20, &backend);
SequentialModule model({&c1, &c2, &relu});

DecompositionOptions o;                        // SPD by default
o.importance_coefficient = 3e-3f;
o.p = 1.0f;
ParameterDecomposition d(model, {&c1, &c2}, &backend, o);
AdamOptimizer opt(1e-3f, &backend);
for (int step = 0; step < steps; ++step) {
    const DecompositionLoss loss = TrainDecomposition(d, NextBatch(), opt);
}

std::vector<std::vector<float>> ci = d.causal_importances(x);   // per layer, (N, C)
std::vector<ImportanceStats> stats = MeasureImportance(d, x);   // alive subcomponents, L0
ComponentAlignment a = AlignComponentsToRows(c1);               // MMCS and ML2R, for toy models
  • The target model is the model itself with every ComponentLinear in target mode, so you don't pass it separately.
  • The output loss compares the masked model's output with the target's: mean squared error, or OutputDivergence::KlOnLogits for logits.
  • Training takes long. The reference toy runs use 40,000 steps of 4,096 inputs, with a learning rate decaying to zero (set_learning_rate on the optimizer).
  • No autograd needed. ComponentLinear::backward() returns the masks' gradients, so the decomposition runs on the model's own backward pass.

docs.title: SPD and VPD
docs.text:
SPD VPD Faithfulness Σ_l ‖W − V U‖² over the number of weights The same, as the loss on the left-over weight Δ = W − V U Reconstruction Every layer masked; then one layer masked at a time For each input, a random number k of the layers use their subcomponents and the rest their original weights. The left-over weight Δ gets its own random mask Adversarial masks — Masks from persistent sources that ascend the loss (PGD), so the decomposition must hold for the worst masks, not only random ones Importance minimality Σ g^p Adds a term that rewards subcomponents used on few inputs. The paper anneals p from 2 to 0.4 during training (set_p)

Choose with o.method = DecompositionMethod::SPD or VPD.

Reading the results: - Alive subcomponents (ImportanceStats::alive): those important (g > 0.1) on some input. Ideally there is one per real mechanism, and the rest die. - L0 of causal importance: how many subcomponents an input uses on average. - MMCS and ML2R (toy models). For each input feature, the best cosine between a subcomponent and the target weight's row, and that subcomponent's norm relative to the row. 1.0 and 1.0 mean the feature has a subcomponent that carries its whole row. An ML2R slightly above 1, as in the results below, means the subcomponent overshoots a little and others cancel the excess.

docs.title: What we found: a toy model of superposition
docs.text:
pulsatrix_spd_toy trains the paper's first test case, then decomposes it: 5 sparse features squeezed through 2 dimensions, x̂ = ReLU(x W Wᵀ + b), with W and Wᵀ decomposed into 20 subcomponents each.

pulsatrix_spd_toy --method spd --steps 40000 --batch 4096
SPD SPD paper VPD (p annealed from 2 to 1) MMCS / ML2R 1.000 / 1.017 1.000 / 0.993 0.993 / 0.672 Alive subcomponents per layer (of 20) 5, 5 5 4, 5 Features with exactly one important subcomponent per layer 5 of 5 5 of 5
  • SPD reproduces the paper. Each feature gets one subcomponent per layer, carrying its whole weight row.
  • VPD, run with SPD's toy settings, merges two of the five features. The VPD report has no toy results to tune against.
  • Faster settings for experiments. A learning rate of 1e-2 and an importance coefficient of 1e-2 reach one subcomponent per feature in 3,000 steps of 1,024.

PULSATRIX_SPD_DUMP=1 makes the tool print every subcomponent's part of each feature's weight row, with its causal importance. That makes problems visible. In development, the first toy target had dropped one of its five features, so that feature's weight row was almost zero. Measures relative to that row were then meaningless.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Language models can't be decomposed. ComponentLinear must be swapped in for a LinearModule, and CausalLM's blocks own theirs.
  • VPD's causal-importance network for language models isn't here. VPD there uses one transformer over every layer's activations; pulsatrix uses SPD's small per-subcomponent networks for both methods.

docs.title: How it's checked
docs.text:
A PyTorch rendering (tools/golden/make_spd_golden.py) matches both methods through the loss, every gradient and an Adam step: - SPD's four losses; - VPD's routing, Δ masks, adversarial masks, frequency term and straight-through clamp.

ComponentLinear matches finite differences. The implementations follow Goodfire's reference code, github.com/goodfire-ai/param-decomp: tag v1 for SPD, and nano_param_decomp/run.py for VPD.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Bushnaq, Braun and Sharkey, "Stochastic Parameter Decomposition", arXiv 2506.20790.
  • Bushnaq et al., "Interpreting Language Model Parameters", Goodfire, 2026 (goodfire.ai/research/interpreting-lm-parameters).
  • Braun et al., "Interpretability in Parameter Space" (APD), arXiv 2501.14926.
  • Elhage et al., "Toy Models of Superposition", Transformer Circuits, 2022.

docs.title: Probes and Concepts
docs.text:
These tools test for concepts you can name. A probe asks whether a layer holds a concept you have labels for. TCAV asks whether a concept, given only by examples, pushes the model towards a class. Both need a control, and this page shows which.

To find the concepts a layer uses without naming them first, train a featurizer. To see where a layer's own channels are in an input, use Concept Relevance Propagation.

The examples collect activations with the hooks described in the overview.

docs.title: Probing a layer for a concept
docs.text:
A linear probe tests whether a concept can be read out of a layer linearly. LinearProbe is a LinearModule(activation_dim, 1) trained with BCEWithLogitsLoss on (activation, label) pairs.

#include "pulsatrix/adam_optimizer.hpp"
#include "pulsatrix/linear_probe.hpp"

// activation_batch: (N, 64) activations; label_batch: (N, 1), values in {0, 1}.
LinearProbe probe(/*activation_dim=*/64, &backend);
AdamOptimizer optimizer(0.01f, &backend);
for (int step = 0; step < 200; ++step) probe.train_step(activation_batch, label_batch, optimizer);
const float accuracy = probe.accuracy(held_out_activations, held_out_labels);
  • High held-out accuracy means the concept is linearly readable.
  • Chance accuracy means it isn't, at least not linearly.
  • A probe reads; it doesn't show the model uses the information.
  • High accuracy can come from the probe rather than the representation. Run a control (below).

docs.title: Controls: the representation or the probe?
docs.text:
probe_controls.hpp trains a multi-class probe, TrainLinearProbe() (standardized features, AdamW, cross-entropy, scored on held-out rows), and gives it two kinds of control.

Hewitt and Liang's control task (EMNLP 2019) gives each token type, such as each word, a random label and keeps it fixed. The labels are drawn from the real labels' distribution. A probe can only learn that by memorizing types, so selectivity, task accuracy minus control accuracy, is what the representation adds beyond memorization.

#include "pulsatrix/probe_controls.hpp"

// features: rows x dim; labels: one class per row; token_types: which word each row is.
const ProbeSelectivity s = MeasureSelectivity(features, dim, labels, /*classes=*/2, token_types,
                                              train, test, &backend);
// s.task.accuracy, s.control.accuracy, s.selectivity, s.train_types

The test shows the difference on two representations of the same 100 token types. In the structured one, each type's label is a linear function of an 8-dimensional vector. The one-hot one only names the type:

Representation Task accuracy Control accuracy Selectivity Structured (8 dimensions) 0.96 0.61 +0.35 One-hot type (100 dimensions) 0.96 0.98 −0.02

Both read the task equally well. Only the structured representation does it without being able to memorize arbitrary labels.

ControlTaskLabels() makes the control labels on their own, for example for a LinearProbe.

When there are few types, compare against a baseline representation. With no more types than dimensions, a linear probe learns any control task. On 20 amino acids it scores 1.0 at every layer of a protein model. CompareToBaseline() trains the same probe on the representation and on a baseline, with the same rows and split, and reports the gain.

Good baselines:

  • one-hot local sequence, SequenceWindowFeatures();
  • the same layer of a randomly initialized model;
  • the raw input.
const std::vector<float> window = SequenceWindowFeatures(sequences, /*window=*/3);
const ProbeGain g = CompareToBaseline(layer, hidden, window, 20 * 7, labels, 2, train, test, &backend);
// g.gain, g.balanced_gain, g.auc_gain (two classes)

The Protein language models guide uses this. Disulfide probes show no gain over local sequence, because they find cysteines. Secondary structure gains 0.20 to 0.25 balanced accuracy.

Recipe: Sparse autoencoder + linear probe.

docs.title: Concepts (TCAV)
docs.text:
TCAV (Kim et al., 2018) asks whether a human concept, given only by examples (striped images, say), pushes a model towards a class. It works in three steps:

  1. A concept activation vector (CAV). TrainCav fits a linear classifier that separates a layer's activations on the concept's examples from its activations on random examples. Its normal, pointing towards the concept, is the CAV.
  2. Sensitivity. Each input's sensitivity is the class logit's gradient at that layer, dotted with the CAV.
  3. The TCAV score. It's the fraction of the class's inputs with positive sensitivity.
#include "pulsatrix/tcav.hpp"

ExplainerContext ctx({&conv1, &relu1, &conv2, &relu2, &flatten, &fc});
// Node i + 1 is module i's output: 4 is relu2's.
const TcavResult r = RunTcav(ctx, /*layer=*/4, /*target=*/zebra, zebra_images, striped_images,
                             random_image_sets, &backend);
// r.mean_score, r.significant, r.test.p_value, r.cav_accuracies

One score means little. A CAV trained against one random set can point anywhere that separates the two sets, and a meaningless direction scores anywhere from 0 to 1. RunTcav follows Kim et al.:

  • It trains a CAV against each of several random sets (at least 3; Kim et al. use many more).
  • It does the same with random sets in place of the concept.
  • A two-sided t-test (StudentTTest) compares the two lists of scores.

A concept is significant at alpha (0.05; divide it by the number of concepts, layers and classes you test). A score near 0 is as significant as one near 1: the concept pushes away from the class.

In the test's network, class 0's logit is 2 h0 − h1. Concepts that raise h0 score 1, and those that raise h1 score 0. Both are significant. A concept that raises only h2, which the logit ignores, isn't, even though its CAVs separate it at over 85%.

Things to know:

  • Use plenty of concept examples. Every CAV of a concept shares its examples, so their sampling noise tilts every CAV the same way. In the test, an ignored concept passed the test in 8 of 40 trials with 30 concept examples, where about 2 are expected by chance. With 300 examples it passed in none.
  • Check the CAV's accuracy. cav_accuracies are measured on held-out examples. Near 0.5, the layer doesn't separate the concept and the CAV means nothing.
  • Logistic regression or difference of means. CavOptions::method chooses. Logistic regression is Kim et al.'s. DifferenceOfMeans needs no fitting and doesn't tilt towards dimensions that separate the two samples only by chance.
  • Models. The models are ExplainerContext chains. TCAV needs the gradient at an inner layer, which the language models don't expose yet.

TCAV starts from concepts people name and asks whether the model uses them. Concept Relevance Propagation goes the other way: it starts from the concepts a layer has learned (its channels) and shows where each one is in an input and what it responds to.

Full API reference: Doxygen: Mechanistic Interpretability

docs.title: Analyzing Representations
docs.text:
These tools describe what a layer does with a set of inputs, without labels: how it compares with another layer or model, which inputs it treats as alike, how many dimensions it uses, and what it looks like in two or three dimensions.

Each takes a matrix with one row per input, (n, width), collected with the hooks described in the overview. Two representations being compared must come from the same n inputs, in the same order.

Your question Tool Section How similar are two layers, two models, or a model before and after fine-tuning? LinearCka, LinearCkaMatrix CKA Does a model order the inputs as a brain recording or a model of the categories does? RsaPermutationTest RSA Which directions do two layers share? Svcca, CanonicalCorrelations SVCCA Which inputs does a layer treat as alike? Do two models agree? NearestNeighbors, MutualKnnAlignment Nearest neighbors Is cosine similarity meaningful here? How many dimensions are used? Anisotropy, MeasureEffectiveRank, TwoNNDimension The shape of a layer What does a layer look like in 2D or 3D? FitPca, RenderProjectionSvg PCA How do I run UMAP or t-SNE on a layer? ExportEmbeddings, ReadNpy UMAP and t-SNE

For clusters, loops and voids, see Topology of representations. To compare two representations' topology next to CKA, use RTD and CompareRepresentations().

Compare against an untrained model. Every number on this page can come from the architecture or the inputs rather than what was learned. Compute it on a NullModelBaseline too.

docs.title: Comparing representations (CKA)
docs.text:
Centered kernel alignment (CKA) measures how similar two representations of the same inputs are: one layer of two models, two layers of one model, a model before and after fine-tuning, or the same layer computed on the CPU and the GPU. Run the same n inputs through both, collect one row per input from each, and compare:

#include "pulsatrix/representation_similarity.hpp"

// layer_a: (n, 768) activations from one model; layer_b: (n, 1024) from another, same n inputs.
const double similarity = LinearCka(layer_a, layer_b);
  • 1 means one representation is a rotation and uniform scaling of the other, plus an offset. The two layers don't need the same width, and their neurons don't need to line up.
  • Near 0 means they are unrelated.
  • Dimensions after the first are flattened, so a convolution's (n, channels, height, width) activations are n vectors. The tensors can be on any device; CKA is computed in double precision on the host.

LinearCkaMatrix(layers_a, layers_b) compares every layer of one model with every layer of another, reusing each layer's work across its row or column. Draw the result as a heatmap:

#include "pulsatrix/viz/svg.hpp"

const CkaMatrix m = LinearCkaMatrix(layers_a, layers_b);
HeatmapDocument doc;
doc.title = "CKA, model A layers × model B layers";
doc.rows = m.rows;
doc.cols = m.cols;
doc.values.assign(m.values.begin(), m.values.end());
std::ofstream("cka.svg") << RenderHeatmapSvg(doc);

Things to know:

  • Use the default, debiased estimator. The original estimator is pulled towards 1 when there are few inputs for the width: two unrelated random representations of 50 inputs with 1,000 features each score 0.95 with it and −0.02 debiased. Pass CkaEstimator::Biased to reproduce numbers from papers that used it. The debiased value can be slightly negative, and needs at least 4 inputs.
  • Compare against an untrained model. Two layers can look similar because of the architecture or the input, not what was learned. In the tests, the second hidden layers of two small networks trained from different seeds score 0.68; one of them against the same network untrained scores 0.10. Run the comparison on a NullModelBaseline too (Baselines).
  • Outliers move it. A few inputs with very large activations can dominate, and CKA can be pushed up or down on purpose (Davari et al., 2022). Check that a result holds on a second set of inputs.
  • A representation that is constant over the inputs has no CKA: the result is NaN.

The implementation matches the reference code of Kornblith et al. (ICML 2019) to 12 decimal places for both estimators.

docs.title: RSA and SVCCA
docs.text:
Two older ways to compare representations are in the same header. Use CKA unless you need one of them.

RSA (representational similarity analysis) describes a representation by how far apart it puts every pair of inputs, its representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM), and correlates two RDMs. Because only the RDM is compared, the other side can be anything that orders the same inputs: another model, a brain recording, or a hand-made matrix that says which inputs share a category.

#include "pulsatrix/representation_similarity.hpp"

const Rdm model = RepresentationalDissimilarity(layer, RdmMetric::Correlation);  // 1 − Pearson
const Rdm categories = ...;  // e.g. 0 within a category, 1 across, in the same pair order
const RsaTestResult r = RsaPermutationTest(model, categories, RdmComparison::Spearman, 999);
// r.similarity: Spearman's correlation of the two RDMs; r.p_value: how often relabeled inputs
// agree as well.
  • The metrics are correlation distance (the RSA default), Euclidean and cosine. RDMs are stored as scipy's pdist stores them, pairs (0, 1), (0, 2), ..., so they can go to or come from Python unchanged; Rdm::at(i, j) reads one.
  • Compare with Spearman (the default) when the two RDMs are on different scales, which is almost always; only the order of the distances counts. Rsa(x, y) does both steps.
  • Test with RsaPermutationTest(), not a correlation's p-value. The distances in an RDM aren't independent (one input's row moves n − 1 of them), so the usual p-value is too small. The test relabels the inputs of one RDM instead. In the tests, two noisy views of four categories agree at 0.83 with p = 1/200, the smallest 199 relabelings can give, and unrelated representations reach p < 0.05 in 3 of 40 trials, about the one in 20 they should.

SVCCA keeps each representation's top singular directions, 99% of the variance by default, and finds the pairs of directions, one in each, that correlate most. The mean of those canonical correlations is the similarity.

const SvccaResult r = Svcca(layer_a, layer_b);  // r.similarity, r.correlations (largest first)
const SvccaResult fixed = Svcca(layer_a, layer_b, SvccaOptions{0.99, 20});  // 20 directions each

Things to know:

  • It is biased upwards, more than CKA. Canonical correlations are fitted to the inputs. Two unrelated 20-dimensional representations score 0.50 with 60 inputs, against −0.02 for debiased CKA, and still 0.09 with 2,000. Use many more inputs than kept directions.
  • It refuses too few inputs. When the kept directions of both add up to the number of inputs or more, some correlations are 1 whatever the data, and Svcca() throws rather than report them. Ask for fewer directions with SvccaOptions::directions.
  • It ignores how a layer weights its directions. CCA is invariant to any invertible linear map: stretching one axis of a layer ten times and shearing another leaves SVCCA at 1, and drops CKA to 0.48 in the tests. Kornblith et al. found CKA better at matching corresponding layers for this reason.
  • CanonicalCorrelations(x, y) is plain CCA, on every direction with variance.

RSA matches independent numpy implementations of scipy's pdist and spearmanr to 12 decimal places, and SVCCA and CCA one written with numpy's SVD and QR to 9.

docs.title: Nearest neighbors
docs.text:
NearestNeighbors() finds, for each input, the k inputs a layer represents most alike, by cosine similarity (the default) or Euclidean distance:

#include "pulsatrix/nearest_neighbors.hpp"

// embeddings: (n, width), a row per input.
NeighborOptions options;
options.k = 5;
options.center = true;  // subtract the mean first; see below
const Neighbors near = NearestNeighbors(embeddings, options);
for (int64_t r = 0; r < near.k; ++r) {
    std::cout << near.index(0, r) << " " << near.score(0, r) << "\n";  // input 0's neighbors, nearest first
}
  • Search another set with NearestNeighbors(queries, points, options), for example new inputs against a labelled reference set.
  • Match items across two sets with MutualNearestNeighbors(a, b, options): the pairs (i, j) where each is among the other's k nearest.
  • Compare two models with MutualKnnAlignment(a, b, options): for each input, the fraction of its k neighbors under one representation that are also its neighbors under the other, averaged. The two can have different widths. With the default options it is the mutual-kNN alignment of Huh et al.'s "Platonic Representation Hypothesis" (2024), and it matches their code exactly. Unrelated representations score about k / (n − 1) by chance, so read a score against that, not against 0. It complements CKA (above): CKA compares the whole geometry, mutual kNN only who is close to whom.

The search is exact, in double precision on the host. It costs about n² × width multiply-adds, so it suits up to tens of thousands of inputs. Ties keep the lower index first.

Things to know:

  • Center cosine similarities. Activations often share a large common component, so every pair's cosine is high and the ranking follows that component. center = true subtracts the points' mean first. It doesn't change Euclidean distances.

  • Check for hubs. In high dimensions a few points become almost everyone's neighbor, and many become nobody's (Radovanović et al., 2010). Neighbor lists, and scores built on them, then say more about the hubs than about the inputs. MeasureHubness(neighbors, n) reports how often each point is a neighbor, and the skewness of those counts: near 0 is even, well above 1 means hubs. For 300 random Gaussian points and k = 5:

    Dimension Skewness The biggest hub is in Never a neighbor 3 −0.04 3% of lists 2% of points 30 2.05 12% of lists 21% of points 300 3.52 20% of lists 36% of points

    Centering also reduces hubness for cosine similarity (Suzuki et al., 2013).

docs.title: The shape of a layer
docs.text:
Three numbers describe a layer's representations of a set of inputs. Each is cheap enough to compute for every layer.

#include "pulsatrix/representation_geometry.hpp"

// layer: (n, width), a row per input.
const double raw = Anisotropy(layer);                     // mean cosine over all pairs
const double centered = Anisotropy(layer, /*center=*/true);
const EffectiveRank rank = MeasureEffectiveRank(layer);  // .effective_rank, .participation_ratio
const TwoNNResult id = TwoNNDimension(layer);            // .dimension, .mle_dimension
  • Anisotropy is the mean cosine similarity between different inputs. Spread-out directions score about 0. Language models' layers often score 0.5 or more (Ethayarajh, 2019): they share a few large directions, so any two inputs look alike by cosine. If raw anisotropy is high and centered anisotropy is near 0, the similarity was the shared direction. Center before comparing by cosine (NeighborOptions::center, above). The test data shows this: rows spread evenly score 0.001, shifting them all along one axis raises that to 0.63, and centering brings it back to −0.003.
  • Effective rank (Roy and Vetterli, 2007) is how many directions the inputs spread along. It's the exponential of the entropy of the normalized singular values, between 1 and the smaller of n and the width. The participation ratio is a coarser count that the largest directions dominate more. Both center by default, because a shared direction would otherwise take up part of the count.
  • TwoNN intrinsic dimension (Facco et al., 2017) is how many dimensions the inputs vary in locally, which can be far below the width. It uses only each point's two nearest neighbors. dimension is the paper's fit and matches scikit-dimension and DADApy. mle_dimension is DADApy's maximum-likelihood version. Exact repeated rows are dropped first and counted in duplicates. In the test, points filling a 2- and a 5-dimensional cube, written in 40 dimensions, give 1.91 and 4.53.

Things to know about TwoNN:

  • Low with too few points. It reads low when the dimension is high for the number of points: tens of dimensions need thousands.
  • Noise raises it. It measures the nearest neighbors' scale, so noise on a low-dimensional surface adds dimensions.
  • Cost. The search is exact, at n² × width.

docs.title: PCA projections
docs.text:
FitPca() finds the directions along which a layer's representations of a set of inputs vary most. PcaProject() places inputs on them, to plot, or to pass fewer dimensions on to another method.

#include <fstream>

#include "pulsatrix/pca.hpp"
#include "pulsatrix/viz/svg.hpp"

// layer: (n, width), a row per input; words and tags: one per input.
const Pca pca = FitPca(layer, /*components=*/3);
const Tensor scores = PcaProject(pca, layer);  // (n, 3)
const ProjectionDocument doc = MakeProjectionDocument(pca, scores, /*labels=*/words, /*groups=*/tags);
std::ofstream("layer.svg") << RenderProjectionSvg(doc);          // PC1 against PC2
std::ofstream("layer13.svg") << RenderProjectionSvg(doc, 0, 2);  // PC1 against PC3
std::ofstream("layer.json") << ToJson(doc);                     // for pulsatrix_svg or HTML

It matches scikit-learn's PCA to 1e-10:

  • The data are centered.
  • Variances divide by n − 1.
  • Each component's largest entry is positive, so the same data always give the same picture.

It runs in double precision, through whichever is smaller of the covariance and the Gram matrix.

  • Plots. RenderProjectionSvg draws two axes on one scale, so distances on the page are distances in the projection. Each axis is captioned with its share of the variance.
  • Points are colored by group or by value, and show their label on hover.
  • RenderProjectionHtml is the zoomable version. With three components it shows the three pairs side by side, the views of a 3D projection.
  • The pulsatrix.projection.v1 document (ToJson) also lets any outside tool draw it.
  • Steering directions. PcaComponent(pca, i) is component i as a unit vector for SteeringHook. One standard deviation along it is sqrt(pca.explained_variance[i]), a natural unit for the coefficient. Then test whether it does anything with MeasureSteering (Steering).
  • Fewer dimensions. PcaReconstruct maps coordinates back. PcaProject(pca, x, /*whiten=*/true) gives every axis variance 1.

Things to know:

  • Check that the picture is stable. Components with close variances can swap or rotate between two samples of the same inputs. PcaSplitHalfOverlap(layer, k) fits each half of the inputs separately and compares the two k-dimensional spans: 1 means the same span, near k / width means unrelated. In the test, points on a plane give 0.9995, the same plane under noise as large as it gives 0.92, and noise alone gives 0.09.
  • Most variance isn't most meaning. In anisotropic layers the first component is often the common direction or a few outlier dimensions (see the shape of a layer). Look at the explained variance ratios, and treat a direction as a hypothesis to test.
  • SubspaceOverlap(a, b, k) compares any two PCAs of the same width, for example the same layer in two models, or before and after fine-tuning.

docs.title: UMAP and t-SNE
docs.text:
pulsatrix doesn't run UMAP or t-SNE. It writes a layer's representations in the formats the tools that do run them read, and reads their coordinates back for its own plots.

#include "pulsatrix/embedding_export.hpp"

// layer: (n, width); words and tags: one per input. The directory must exist.
ExportEmbeddings("layer6", layer, {{"word", words}, {"tag", tags}});
// layer6/vectors.npy, layer6/vectors.tsv, layer6/metadata.tsv
  • In Python: np.load("layer6/vectors.npy") goes straight into umap.UMAP().fit_transform, openTSNE.TSNE().fit or scikit-learn's TSNE. WriteNpy and SerializeNpy write any tensor the same way, float32 with its shape.
  • In the browser, with nothing to install: load vectors.tsv and metadata.tsv into the Embedding Projector (projector.tensorflow.org), which runs UMAP, t-SNE and PCA and colors points by any metadata column.
  • Back in pulsatrix: save the coordinates with np.save, read them with ReadNpy, and make a projection document, which the PCA views draw:
const Tensor xy = ReadNpy("layer6/umap.npy", &backend);  // (n, 2), from Python
const ProjectionDocument doc = MakeProjectionDocument(xy, "umap", words, tags);
std::ofstream("layer6_umap.svg") << RenderProjectionSvg(doc);

Things to know:

  • These plots keep neighbors, not distances. The gaps between clusters, the clusters' sizes and their densities carry little meaning, and shapes can come from the settings alone (perplexity, n_neighbors, min_dist). The views say so under every plot whose method is umap, tsne, t-sne or opentsne. Ask questions about distances of PCA, and about neighbors of nearest neighbors, which measures them directly.
  • Run them more than once. Both start from random positions. A cluster that appears in one run and not another, or under one perplexity and not another, isn't evidence of anything.
  • Reduce first if the layer is wide. Running PCA to about 50 dimensions first (FitPca, PcaProject, then export the scores) is standard for t-SNE, and makes both faster.
  • The reader takes what numpy writes for float arrays: float32 or float64, C or Fortran order, format versions 1 to 3. It rejects anything else, including pickled objects, with an error rather than a guess, and is fuzzed (tools/fuzz/npy_fuzz.cpp).

Full API reference: Doxygen: Mechanistic Interpretability

docs.title: Steering
docs.text:
Steering adds a direction to a model's residual stream during the forward pass, to push its behavior one way: more positive sentiment, a different language, a hydrophobic residue. It is the causal counterpart of a probe. A probe asks whether a concept can be read from a layer; steering asks whether writing a direction changes what the model does.

It is also easy to fool yourself with. An average effect at one large coefficient can look like success when any perturbation of that size would do the same, and many individual inputs may move the wrong way. MeasureSteering reports what you need to tell the difference.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
#include "pulsatrix/steering.hpp"

// 1. A direction: the difference of means between activations with and without the concept.
//    with_concept, without_concept: row-major (N, d) activations from the same layer.
std::vector<float> v = DifferenceOfMeans(with_concept, without_concept, /*d=*/hidden);

// 2. Steer: add coefficient × v to the residual stream after block 4.
model->set_hidden_state_hook(SteeringHook(/*position=*/4, v, /*coefficient=*/1.0f));
// ... generate or score ...
model->set_hidden_state_hook({});

// 3. Measure how reliably it works.
SteeringReport r = MeasureSteering(
    [&](int64_t i, const HiddenStateHook& hook) {
        model->set_hidden_state_hook(hook);
        const double b = Behavior(*model, inputs[i]);   // a number steering should raise
        model->set_hidden_state_hook({});
        return b;
    },
    static_cast<int64_t>(inputs.size()), /*position=*/4, v);
  • The direction. The difference of means is the default, and usually the better choice. A featurizer's decoder direction is the alternative (FeaturizerDirection(sae, feature)); on AxBench (Wu et al.) it usually steers worse.
  • The behavior is any number steering should raise: a logit difference, a log-probability, a probe's score. MeasureSteering calls it once per input and coefficient.
  • Options (SteeringOptions):
  • the coefficients to try. The default is −0.5, −0.25, 0, 0.25, 0.5, with 0 as the unsteered baseline. Keep the range well below the residual stream's norm: in the example below, ±2 was large enough to disrupt ESM-2 and fake a success.
  • how many random directions to use as the control (default 3);
  • a seed.
  • SteeringHook takes an optional row mask, to steer only some positions.

docs.title: Reading the report
docs.text:
Following Tan et al., the report doesn't stop at the mean effect:

Field Meaning steerability Each input's least-squares slope of behavior against the coefficient mean_steerability, steerability_sd Their mean and spread over inputs anti_steerable_fraction The share of inputs with a negative slope: steering moves them the wrong way random_mean_steerability, random_max_abs_steerability The same for random directions of the same norm: their mean, and the largest magnitude over_random Mean steerability divided by random_max_abs_steerability. Below about 1, the direction does no better than noise

A checklist before calling a steering vector successful: 1. over_random well above 1. 2. A small anti-steerable share. 3. Behavior that rises roughly linearly with the coefficient, in both directions. If it rises at both −1 and +1, the perturbation is breaking the model, not steering it. 4. Small coefficients relative to the residual stream's norm, so you stay where the model is linear.

docs.title: A worked example: a steering vector that fails its checks
docs.text:
pulsatrix_steer_esm steers ESM-2 8M's layer 4 toward transmembrane residues:

python3 tools/plm/fetch_swissprot_annotations.py data/swissprot
pulsatrix_steer_esm models/esm2_t6_8M_UR50D --annotations data/swissprot/annotated.jsonl --out steer/ \
    --layer 4 --max-coefficient 2

It writes the per-coefficient means (steering.csv) and each protein's slope (steerability.csv). --max-coefficient sets the range, from −C to C; it defaults to 0.5. The ESM-2 download is in Finding features.

The setup: - Direction: the difference of means between transmembrane residues and the rest, over 800 proteins. Its norm is 9.1, against a mean residual norm of 29. The alternative is the TopK SAE feature that best matches transmembrane residues (F1 0.64 in this run's SAE), scaled to the same norm. - Behavior: the log-probability of a hydrophobic residue minus a polar one, at masked positions. It should rise. - Inputs: 100 held-out soluble proteins.

Coefficients Direction Mean steerability Anti-steerable over_random ±2 Difference of means +0.087 18% 0.29 ±2 SAE feature +0.023 32% 0.08 ±0.5 Difference of means −0.139 66% −1.41 ±0.5 SAE feature +0.002 46% 0.02 ±0.25 Difference of means −0.208 78% −1.96
  • At ±2 the average looks like success, and it isn't steering. The added vector has norm 18, and random directions of the same norm move the behavior more. The behavior also rises at both −1 and +1, which no linear direction explains.
  • At small coefficients the difference of means steers the wrong way. It makes soluble proteins' masked positions less hydrophobic, for about three proteins in four.
  • The SAE feature doesn't steer at all at any scale.

A mean effect at ±2 alone would have reported a success. The per-input slopes, the anti-steerable share and the random control show there is none. A probe that reads a concept doesn't give a direction that writes it. For this reason the tool defaults to ±0.5.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tan et al., "Analyzing the Generalization and Reliability of Steering Vectors", NeurIPS 2024.
  • Wu et al., "AxBench", arXiv 2501.17148.

docs.title: Topology of Representations
docs.text:
Persistent homology measures the shape of a set of points: its clusters, the loops they form, and the voids they enclose, and how long each lasts as the scale grows. Applied to a layer's activations, it asks questions the tools in Analyzing representations can't: does a layer arrange the days of the week on a circle, and does that circle survive noise and a random-network control?

pulsatrix builds this as a pipeline, one stage at a time:

PointCloud → distances → filtration → persistence diagram → numbers and plots

This page grows with each stage. So far it covers the point cloud, the distances, the diagrams (H0, then loops, voids and higher), how to compare diagrams, how to turn them into numbers, landmarks for large clouds, whether a feature is real, and comparing two representations' topology.

docs.title: From activations to a point cloud
docs.text:
PointCloud gathers a layer's activations, batch by batch, into one set of points. Each point remembers the sample and position it came from, so a loop found later can be traced back to the inputs that form it.

#include "pulsatrix/tda/point_cloud.hpp"

PointCloud cloud({PointPooling::PerPosition});  // one point per token
model->set_hidden_state_hook([&](int64_t position, const Tensor& h) {
    if (position == 6) cloud.add(h);             // (1, tokens, width)
    return h;
});
for (const std::string& text : corpus) (void)model->forward(Encode(text));
// cloud.size() points of cloud.dimension() == width.
// cloud.origins()[i].sample is the text, .position the token.

How a sample becomes points is the one choice to make:

PointPooling Points per sample Use it for Flatten (the default) One, every dimension after the batch flattened An MLP layer, a classifier's logits PerPosition One per token or pixel The geometry of token representations Mean, Max One, pooled over the positions A summary of an encoder's whole input Last One, the last position A causal language model's summary of the whole input
  • The feature axis. For every pooling but Flatten, PointCloudOptions::feature_axis says which axis holds the features. The default, the last axis, suits a sequence model's (batch, tokens, width). Use 1 for a convolution's (batch, channels, height, width); its pixels then become the positions, in row-major order.
  • Batches of different lengths. The first batch fixes the points' dimension. Later batches can have any number of positions, so texts of different lengths go in one at a time. Sample numbers keep counting across batches.
  • Snapshots. cloud.add(snapshot, node) adds one node of an ExplainerContext snapshot. MakePointCloud(snapshots, node) builds a cloud from several.
  • Checks. A batch with a NaN or infinity, or of the wrong dimension, throws and adds nothing. Mean sums in double precision.

cloud.ToTensor(&backend) gives the points as an (n, dimension) tensor for the stages that follow.

docs.title: Distances, with an error bar
docs.text:
Persistent homology sees the points only through their pairwise distances. PairwiseDistances() computes them as |x|² + |y|² − 2 x·y, with the dot products from one GEMM on the cloud's backend (CPU, HIP or CUDA):

#include "pulsatrix/tda/distance_matrix.hpp"

const DistanceMatrix d = PairwiseDistances(cloud, &backend);
// d.values: the n (n − 1) / 2 distances, in scipy's pdist order; d.at(i, j) reads one.
// d.error_bound: every stored distance is within this of the exact one.

Why the error bound. In float32 that formula cancels for points close together, relative to their distance from the origin. The result can be wrong in every digit, and since persistent homology is all about small distances (when do two points join?), that matters. So every DistanceMatrix carries a certified bound: |stored − exact| ≤ error_bound for every pair.

  • It's rigorous. It comes from the standard error analysis of a float32 dot product (at most γ_d ‖x‖ ‖y‖, whatever order the GEMM sums in), plus the double-precision steps and the final rounding. It assumes the GEMM accumulates in float32, not TF32 or bf16.
  • It carries through. Persistence diagrams are stable: a diagram computed from these distances is within error_bound, in bottleneck distance, of the exact one. Later stages add their own errors to it.
  • When it's large, center. Points sharing a large offset, as in an anisotropic layer, make the bound large. DistanceOptions::center subtracts the mean first, which leaves the distances unchanged. In the tests, points spread by 0.01 per coordinate, sitting 1,000 from the origin, get a bound bigger than a tenth of their distances. Centered, it shrinks over a hundredfold, to under a thousandth.
  • Or compute exactly. DistanceMethod::Exact sums squared differences in double on the host. Its bound is the float32 rounding of the result, but it costs n² × d on the CPU.

Other options:

  • normalize scales every point to unit length first. The distance is then √(2 − 2 cos), a metric that orders pairs as cosine similarity does.
  • block_rows sets how many rows each GEMM computes. The device holds the points and one block at a time; by default a block has at most 2²⁴ entries.

Storing n (n − 1) / 2 float32 values takes 50 MB for 5,000 points. Persistent homology above H0 can't use many more points than that anyway; landmarks choose which ones to keep.

docs.title: Clusters across scales (H0)
docs.text:
Grow a ball around every point. At scale 0 each point is its own component. As the scale grows, two components merge when the shortest edge between them appears, until one is left. H0 persistence records those merges: one pair (born at 0, dies at the merge scale) per merge, and one pair that never dies.

That is single-linkage clustering, and the merge scales are the edge lengths of a minimum spanning tree. ComputeH0() finds the tree exactly with Prim's algorithm, in O(n²) time:

#include "pulsatrix/tda/h0.hpp"

const H0Result h0 = ComputeH0(PairwiseDistances(cloud, &backend));
// h0.diagram.pairs: (0, merge scale) per merge, then (0, ∞). h0.diagram.error_bound is the
// distances' bound: the diagram is within it of the exact one, in bottleneck distance.
// h0.edges: the tree's n − 1 edges, shortest first; edge k is the k-th merge.
const std::vector<int64_t> clusters = SingleLinkageClusters(h0.edges, cloud.size(), /*threshold=*/0.5);
  • Long-lived pairs are clusters. A pair that dies late means a group that stays apart from the rest over a wide range of scales. SingleLinkageClusters() cuts the tree at a scale and labels the groups. Each edge's endpoints, through cloud.origins(), name the inputs a merge joins.
  • Duplicate points give zero-length edges. They stay in edges but not in the diagram, which leaves out zero-persistence pairs as Ripser does.
  • Ties in length break by the lower point index, so the tree is the same on every platform. Its lengths, which are all the diagram uses, are the same for every minimum tree.

H0 alone says little. It is a function of the minimum spanning tree, so it sees roughly what nearest-neighbor distances see. Many recent papers on the topology of language models use only H0. Before trusting such a result, check it against plain nearest-neighbor statistics. Loops and voids (H1, H2) are where persistent homology sees something new.

docs.title: Loops and voids (H1, H2 and up)
docs.text:
ComputeRipsPersistence() computes the diagrams of the Vietoris–Rips filtration in every dimension up to max_dimension. A simplex joins the complex at its diameter, and loops (H1) and voids (H2) form and fill in as the scale grows:

#include "pulsatrix/tda/rips_persistence.hpp"

RipsOptions options;
options.max_dimension = 2;   // H0, H1 and H2
const RipsResult r = ComputeRipsPersistence(PairwiseDistances(cloud, &backend), options);
for (const RipsFeature& loop : r.features[1]) {
    // loop.pair.birth, loop.pair.death; r.diagrams[1] has the same pairs.
    // loop.birth_edge, loop.death_edge: the edges whose lengths are the birth and the death.
}
  • Where a feature comes from. Each feature names its critical edges. The birth edge is the longest edge of the simplex that creates the feature; the death edge is the longest edge of the one that fills it in. Their endpoints, through cloud.origins(), are inputs.
  • Representative cocycles. With RipsOptions::cocycles, each feature in H1 and up comes with a cocycle: a value on edges (for H1) whose coboundary vanishes on every triangle present before the death. A loop's cocycle is nonzero summed around the loop. Circular coordinates, which place points on the loop, are built from it.
  • Coefficients. coefficient is the prime p of the field Z/p, 2 by default. Diagrams over different primes differ only for spaces with torsion, such as the projective plane. Circular coordinates need a prime above 2, to lift the cocycle to the integers.
  • The threshold. By default it is the enclosing radius, the smallest over points of the distance to the farthest one. There the complex is a cone, so every loop and void has died and nothing is cut short. With a lower threshold, features still alive at it are reported as essential (death ∞).

How it is computed. It follows the algorithm of Bauer's Ripser (2021), written for pulsatrix rather than vendored:

  • persistent cohomology, which pairs the same intervals as homology;
  • simplices named by their index in the combinatorial number system, with coboundaries enumerated on demand rather than stored;
  • clearing, and zero-persistence apparent pairs, which are settled without any reduction.

On a CPU (Release build, points in 3 dimensions) it takes:

Points Dimensions Time Memory 1,000 H0, H1 0.25 s 2,000 H0, H1 1.2 s 300 H0 to H2 0.5 s 600 H0 to H2 4.1 s 125 MB peak for the whole run

Cost grows quickly with the number of points and the dimension. Above a few thousand points for H1, or about a thousand for H2, choose landmarks first.

How it is checked. Nothing here relies on another library's output:

  • A theorem. Evenly spaced points on a circle have a known Rips complex at every scale (Adamaszek and Adams, 2017). For 12 points: one loop from the side length to the chord of 4 steps, then exactly three voids from there to the chord of 5 steps.
  • Betti numbers from scratch. For every subset of 7 random points, at every scale, the ranks of the boundary matrices over Z/2 and Z/3 give the Betti numbers. The pairs alive at that scale must match them in every dimension.
  • The Euler characteristic. On 8 random points it matches at every scale.
  • The cocycle condition, and the winding of a circle's cocycle.
  • H0 matches the minimum spanning tree.

docs.title: Comparing diagrams
docs.text:
Two diagrams, say of the same layer in two models, two seeds, or before and after fine-tuning, are compared by matching their points. Each point goes either to a point of the other diagram or to the diagonal, where a feature of zero persistence would sit:

#include "pulsatrix/tda/diagram_distance.hpp"

const Certified<double> d = BottleneckDistance(base.diagrams[1], tuned.diagrams[1]);
// d.value: the largest move in the best matching.
// d.bound(): the exact diagrams' distance is within this of d.value; d.terms itemize it.
const double w2 = WassersteinDistance(base.diagrams[1], tuned.diagrams[1], /*order=*/2);
  • Bottleneck distance is the smallest possible largest move. It is the distance the stability theorem uses (Chazal, de Silva and Oudot, 2014): if two clouds' distance matrices differ by at most e, their Rips diagrams are within e. The tests check this on random clouds and perturbations, in H0 and H1, and the bound comes close to tight.
  • Wasserstein distance W_q is the q-th root of the smallest sum of q-th powers of the moves. It counts every feature, where the bottleneck counts only the worst one. As q grows it approaches the bottleneck.
  • Moves are measured in the L∞ norm, as in the stability theorem, so a point (b, d) is (d − b) / 2 from the diagonal. Essential features are matched to each other by birth. If two diagrams have different numbers of them, the distance is infinite.

Certified values. Certified<T> holds a value and the error terms behind it, each with its source. A bottleneck distance carries both diagrams' error_bounds: by the triangle inequality, the distance between the exact diagrams is within their sum. So a difference between two layers is real only if it exceeds d.bound().

The Wasserstein distance isn't certified. An error of e in every distance can move it by up to e times the q-th root of the number of points, so a single bound would mean little.

Both are exact. The bottleneck distance uses a binary search over candidate values, each tested by a Hopcroft–Karp matching, and is comfortable up to a few hundred points per diagram. The Wasserstein distance uses the Hungarian algorithm, which takes (n₁ + n₂)³ time, so up to about a thousand points in all. Both match brute force over every matching on small diagrams.

docs.title: Diagrams as numbers
docs.text:
A probe, a t-test or a plot needs a fixed-size vector, not a set of points. Four standard vectorizations are in tda/vectorization.hpp:

#include "pulsatrix/tda/vectorization.hpp"

const std::vector<double> grid = LinearGrid(0.0, r.threshold, 100);
const std::vector<int64_t> betti = BettiCurve(r.diagrams[1], grid);           // loops alive at each t
const Certified<PersistenceLandscape> l = ComputePersistenceLandscape(r.diagrams[1], grid, /*layers=*/5);
const PersistenceImage image = ComputePersistenceImage(r.diagrams[1], image_options);
const double entropy = PersistentEntropy(r.diagrams[1]);
Vectorization What it is Stable? Betti curve How many features are alive at each scale No: a point crossing a grid value changes it by 1 Persistence landscape (Bubenik, 2015) λ_k(t), the k-th largest "tent" min(t − b, d − t) at each t Yes: within the bottleneck distance, at every t. Certified. Persistence image (Adams et al., 2017) Points at (birth, persistence), weighted by persistence, blurred by a Gaussian, integrated over pixels Under the 1-Wasserstein distance, not the bottleneck Persistent entropy The Shannon entropy of the lifetimes, in nats Not in general
  • Prefer landscapes when the result has to hold up. They are the only one of the four that inherits the stability theorem. ComputePersistenceLandscape returns a Certified value: the exact diagram's landscapes are within bound() of these at every grid point.
  • Fix the image's ranges when comparing. By default a persistence image takes its birth and persistence ranges from its own diagram. Images of two diagrams are comparable only with birth_max, persistence_max and sigma set the same for both.
  • Essential features are left out of everything except the Betti curve, where they count from their birth on. Report how many there are (essential_count()) alongside.

docs.title: Landmarks for large clouds
docs.text:
A layer's activations over a dataset can be 100,000 points, far more than H1 or H2 can handle. FarthestPointLandmarks() picks a subset that covers the whole cloud. Each landmark is chosen greedily as the point farthest from those already picked:

#include "pulsatrix/tda/landmarks.hpp"

LandmarkOptions options;
options.count = 1000;            // or options.radius: stop once every point is that close
const Landmarks l = FarthestPointLandmarks(cloud, &backend, options);
const Tensor subset = LandmarkPoints(cloud.ToTensor(&backend), l);
const RipsResult r = ComputeRipsPersistence(PairwiseDistances(subset), rips_options);
const PersistenceDiagram loops = WithSubsamplingBound(r.diagrams[1], l);
// loops.error_bound now bounds the bottleneck distance to the diagram of *all* the points.
  • The certified bound. Every point is within the covering radius ε of a landmark, so the landmarks' Rips diagrams are within 2ε of the whole cloud's in bottleneck distance. l.covering_radius is a Certified value whose term is the float32 error of the distances behind it. WithSubsamplingBound() adds 2 × (ε + that error) to a diagram's own bound. A feature of the landmarks with persistence well above twice that is a feature of the cloud.
  • Choosing the count. l.insertion_radii[k] is the covering radius just before landmark k was added. It only decreases; plot it and stop where it flattens. Greedy selection is within a factor of 2 of the best possible covering radius for the same count (Gonzalez, 1985). The tests check this against brute force on small clouds.
  • Cost. Each landmark costs one GEMM of all the points against it, on the cloud's backend, so k landmarks take O(n k d). The n × n distance matrix is never formed.
  • Ties go to the lowest index. options.first sets the first landmark. options.center shrinks the float32 error when the points share a large offset, as it does for distances.
  • Where each point went. l.nearest[i] and l.distance_to_nearest[i] give each point's landmark. Use them to carry labels or inputs over from the landmarks back to the whole cloud.

In the tests, 50 landmarks of a noisy circle of 300 points give an H1 diagram within its certified bound of the full diagram, and the circle's loop persists more than four times longer than the bound.

docs.title: Is a feature real?
docs.text:
A diagram of pure noise is full of short-lived loops, and some always live longer than the rest. Before reporting a loop, test it. tda/significance.hpp has three tests, each answering a slightly different question.

The universal null: one diagram, a p-value per feature. Bobrowski and Skraba (2023) found that the death/birth ratios of noise follow one distribution, whatever the noise came from, once normalized: ℓ = log log(death / birth) − L̄ − γ, where L̄ is the diagram's mean of log log(death / birth) and γ is Euler's constant. Under the null, ℓ follows a left-skewed Gumbel distribution, so a feature's p-value is exp(−e^ℓ). Bonferroni's correction then splits α over the features.

#include "pulsatrix/tda/significance.hpp"

const UniversalNullResult u = UniversalNullTest(r.diagrams[1], /*alpha=*/0.05);
for (const FeatureSignificance& f : u.features) {
    if (f.significant) { /* r.features[1][f.index] is a real loop */ }
}
  • It's a conjecture, supported by the authors' experiments on many distributions and real data, not a theorem. The constants are theirs for Rips filtrations (A = 1).
  • It needs a mostly-noise diagram. L̄ comes from the diagram itself, so use diagrams with hundreds of features or more. Point sets spaced too evenly, such as lattices, don't follow it.
  • In the tests, the p-values of the loops of uniform noise are calibrated (about a tenth fall below 0.1, and half below 0.5), and Bonferroni flags at most one of their 300-odd loops. A ring with clutter around it is flagged; the same ring with uniform points inside it isn't, since those points fill the loop in at once.

The bootstrap band: how far the diagram moves under resampling. BootstrapBand() resamples the points with replacement, computes each resample's diagram, and takes the 1 − α quantile c of their bottleneck distances to the original (Fasy et al., 2014). Features with persistence above 2c lie outside the band. Resamples reuse the distance matrix, so nothing is recomputed, but each one is a full Rips computation. Fasy et al. prove coverage for distance-function filtrations; for Rips diagrams the band is the standard heuristic.

Baselines: is this more structure than a cloud with nothing in it? Compute a statistic, such as MaxPersistence() of H1, on the data and on clouds with no structure, then take BaselinePValue(), the rank p-value:

  • GaussianBaseline(points, count, seed) draws a Gaussian cloud with the same mean and covariance (one GEMM, and the covariance's rank is kept, so a cloud in a plane gives a baseline in the same plane);
  • for a random-network baseline, collect the same layer's activations from a NullModelBaseline copy of the model.

With m baselines the smallest p-value is 1 / (m + 1): use 19 for p = 0.05, 99 for 0.01.

Use more than one. The universal null is cheapest, and the bootstrap needs no conjecture. The random-network baseline is the one that asks whether the structure was learned.

For all of them on a real model, see the recipe Is the shape real?. It tests the calendar circle in SmolLM2-135M and Llama-3.2-1B, and one of its lessons is a caution: on points that come in tight clusters, the largest death/birth ratio can pick loops inside the clusters rather than the ring through them.

docs.title: Seeing the result
docs.text:
viz/topology_documents.hpp saves diagrams as a pulsatrix.persistence_diagram.v1 document, with each dimension's certified error bound and any test results. viz/topology_views.hpp draws the document three ways:

  • RenderPersistenceDiagramSvg: birth against death. A gray band along the diagonal covers persistence up to twice the error bound, which errors in the distances alone could explain. Features that never die sit on a dashed ∞ line.
  • RenderBarcodeSvg: one bar per feature, longest first, with ±error-bound whiskers.
  • RenderBettiCurveSvg: how many features are alive at each scale. The error bound doesn't cover it, since short features can come and go; the figure says so.

With a test attached, significant features are drawn filled (diagram) or solid (barcode), and the rest hollow or faint:

#include "pulsatrix/viz/topology_views.hpp"

PersistenceDiagramDocument doc = ToPersistenceDiagramDocument(r, "Layer 12, weekday tokens");
AttachSignificance(doc, 1, UniversalNullTest(r.diagrams[1]));   // p-values on H1
std::ofstream("diagram.svg") << RenderPersistenceDiagramSvg(doc);
std::ofstream("doc.json") << ToJson(doc);   // later: pulsatrix_svg doc.json --view barcode

On the command line: pulsatrix_svg doc.json --view diagram|barcode|betti [--dims 1]. There is no HTML view yet.

docs.title: Comparing two representations' topology (RTD)
docs.text:
CKA compares two representations' whole geometry at once. When most of the variance is in a few large distances, it can call two layers alike although one splits a cluster that the other keeps whole. Representation Topology Divergence (Barannikov, Trofimov et al., 2022) compares the clusters and loops at every scale:

#include "pulsatrix/tda/rtd.hpp"

const RtdResult r = Rtd(layer_a, layer_b);   // rows: the same inputs, in the same order
// r.rtd: 0 for the same topology; larger means more clusters and loops differ, and by more.

const RepresentationComparison c = CompareRepresentations(layer_a, layer_b);
// c.cka, c.mutual_knn, c.rtd.rtd: three views side by side.
  • How it works. Each representation's distances are divided by their 0.9 quantile, so scale doesn't count. A Vietoris–Rips filtration on two copies of the inputs then mixes the two sets of distances. Its H1 barcode, the R-Cross-Barcode, holds a bar for each cluster that merges at one scale in one representation and at another scale in the other. RTD is the total length of those bars, averaged over both directions and over random batches of 500 inputs (RtdOptions, as in the paper's Algorithm 2).
  • What it guarantees. The cross-barcode of identical representations is empty. Against distances that are all 0, it is the ordinary barcode one dimension down (the paper's Theorem 2.1). The tests check both exactly, and that rotation and scale leave RTD near 0.
  • In the tests, two clusters 40 apart, each then split in two, keep CKA above 0.9, while RTD rises almost fivefold over a jittered copy. Mutual-kNN alignment drops too: it sees the neighbors change.
  • CrossBarcode(w, w~, dimension) gives the barcode itself, for your own distances (not normalized), to see which clusters differ.
  • Cost. Each batch is a Rips computation on twice the batch size.

Full API reference: Doxygen: Topological Data Analysis

docs.title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
docs.text:
Use this section when you want a neural network to work together with logical rules. You can train a network so its outputs satisfy rules such as "if A then not B". You can also feed a network's output into a rule-based (Datalog) program and trace the result back to the network's input.

There are two layers:

  • A fuzzy-logic core treats truth as a number in [0, 1] instead of true/false, so logical rules become differentiable and you can train against them with gradient descent. It follows the design of Logic Tensor Networks.
  • A Datalog engine derives new facts from rules. A neural network's output can serve as the weight of one input fact.

docs.title: Which part should I use?
docs.text: Goal Use Train a network so its predictions obey logical constraints Fuzzy-logic core: ConjunctionModule, DisjunctionModule, NegationModule, AggregatorModule, SatisfactionLoss Derive facts from rules and a fact list (true/false) FactDatabase + semi_naive_evaluate Derive facts whose confidence is a number WeightedFactDatabase<T> + semi_naive_evaluate_weighted Explain which input facts a derived fact depends on propagate_relevance_weighted (Datalog LRP) Connect a network's output to a Datalog derivation, end to end NeuralPredicateDatalogBridge

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text:
Fuzzy-logic core. Each operator works on truth degrees in [0, 1] and is a Module with forward()/backward():

  • ConjunctionModule / DisjunctionModule: fuzzy AND / OR. A t-norm is a fuzzy AND formula; a t-conorm is the matching OR. Pick one with ConjunctionModule::TNorm or DisjunctionModule::TConorm (Product, Lukasiewicz, Godel).
  • NegationModule: fuzzy NOT (1 - x).
  • AggregatorModule: a differentiable "for all" over many examples, using the p-mean agg_p(x) = (mean(x^p))^(1/p).
  • SatisfactionLoss: loss = 1 - agg_p(truth_values). Minimizing it maximizes how well the rules hold.
  • ToyKnowledgeBase: a small worked example that chains the above into one trainable rule, A(x) -> not(B(x)).

Datalog engine. Datalog is a simple rule language: head :- body1, body2, ... means "the head is true when every body atom is true". The engine supports rules without function symbols, where every head variable also appears in the body (safe rules), so evaluation always terminates.

  • Term / Atom / Rule: the building blocks of a rule.
  • FactDatabase: a set of true facts.
  • naive_evaluate / semi_naive_evaluate: apply rules until no new facts appear. Both give identical results; semi-naive is faster because each round only revisits newly derived facts.
  • WeightedFactDatabase<T>, naive_evaluate_weighted, semi_naive_evaluate_weighted: the same engine with a number attached to each fact. The template argument is a semiring (a pair of "combine alternatives" and "combine requirements" operations), such as BooleanSemiring or RealSemiring<T>.
  • DualSemiring<T>: a semiring that also carries a derivative. One evaluation gives a derived fact's weight and its derivative with respect to an input fact's weight.
  • propagate_relevance_weighted (datalog_lrp.hpp): an LRP rule for Datalog derivations. It splits a derived fact's relevance across its alternative derivations and then across each derivation's body facts. For LRP itself, see LRP.

Neural-predicate bridge. NeuralPredicateDatalogBridge uses a small network (LinearModule + sigmoid) to produce one Datalog fact's weight. A derived fact's weight, and its LRP relevance, then depend on the network's output.

Full API reference: Doxygen: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning

docs.title: Training a rule with the fuzzy-logic core
docs.text:
#include "pulsatrix/cpu_backend.hpp"
#include "pulsatrix/neuro_symbolic_toy_kb.hpp"
#include "pulsatrix/sgd_optimizer.hpp"

using namespace pulsatrix;

CPUBackend backend;
ToyKnowledgeBase kb(&backend, /*p=*/2.0f);  // rule A(x) -> not(B(x)), as not(A(x)) or not(B(x))
SGDOptimizer optimizer(0.1f);

Tensor x(Shape({4, 1}), &backend, {-1.5f, -0.5f, 0.5f, 1.5f});  // 4 example inputs
for (int epoch = 0; epoch < 500; ++epoch) {
    float loss = kb.train_step(x, optimizer);  // forward + backward + SGD update
}

What's happening: ToyKnowledgeBase has two small networks, A(x) and B(x) (each a LinearModule followed by a sigmoid). It rewrites A(x) -> not(B(x)) as not(A(x)) or not(B(x)), using the rule P -> Q equals not(P) or Q. Two NegationModules and a DisjunctionModule (Product t-conorm) compute the rule's truth for each input. SatisfactionLoss then turns those into one loss. Every step has forward()/backward(), so the whole rule trains with ordinary gradient descent and no separate solver.

To run it: cmake --build build --target neuro_symbolic_toy_kb_demo. The demo (examples/neuro_symbolic_toy_kb_demo.cpp) trains for 500 epochs and prints the loss and satisfaction as it goes.

docs.title: Deriving facts with the Datalog engine
docs.text:
#include "pulsatrix/datalog_engine.hpp"

using namespace pulsatrix::datalog;

Term X = Term::make_variable("X"), Y = Term::make_variable("Y"), Z = Term::make_variable("Z");
auto c = [](const char* name) { return Term::make_constant(name); };

// ancestor(X,Y) :- edge(X,Y).
// ancestor(X,Y) :- edge(X,Z), ancestor(Z,Y).
std::vector<Rule> rules = {
    Rule(Atom("ancestor", {X, Y}), {Atom("edge", {X, Y})}),
    Rule(Atom("ancestor", {X, Y}), {Atom("edge", {X, Z}), Atom("ancestor", {Z, Y})}),
};

FactDatabase facts;
facts.insert(Atom("edge", {c("a"), c("b")}));
facts.insert(Atom("edge", {c("b"), c("c")}));

FactDatabase result = semi_naive_evaluate(rules, facts);
bool derived = result.contains(Atom("ancestor", {c("a"), c("c")}));  // true

What's happening: semi_naive_evaluate applies the rules repeatedly until no new facts appear. The result holds the input facts plus every derived ancestor fact. Input facts must be ground, meaning they contain no variables; insert() throws otherwise.

docs.title: Bridging a neural predicate into a Datalog derivation
docs.text:
#include "pulsatrix/cpu_backend.hpp"
#include "pulsatrix/neuro_symbolic_datalog_bridge.hpp"

using namespace pulsatrix::datalog;
using pulsatrix::CPUBackend;
using pulsatrix::Shape;
using pulsatrix::Tensor;

CPUBackend backend;
NeuralPredicateDatalogBridge bridge(&backend);

// edge(a,b)'s weight comes from a neural predicate; edge(a,c), edge(b,d), edge(c,d) are
// constants. Program: ancestor(X,Y) :- edge(X,Y).  ancestor(X,Y) :- edge(X,Z), ancestor(Z,Y).
Tensor x(Shape({1, 1}), &backend, {0.5f});
NeuralPredicateQueryResult query = bridge.evaluate(x);
// query.query_weight: ancestor(a,d)'s derived weight
// query.grad_wrt_predicate_output: its derivative w.r.t. edge(a,b)'s weight

bridge.backward();  // accumulates the predicate's LinearModule weight/bias gradients

NeuralPredicateRelevanceResult relevance = bridge.propagate_relevance(/*relevance_seed=*/1.0);
// relevance.base_fact_relevance: each base fact's share of the relevance
// relevance.relevance_wrt_x: edge(a,b)'s share, carried on into the raw input x

What's happening: evaluate() runs weighted Datalog evaluation with DualSemiring<double>. In one pass it computes ancestor(a,d)'s weight and its derivative with respect to the network's output.

propagate_relevance() then runs the Datalog LRP rule back through the derivation. Because edge(a,b) comes from the network, its relevance continues through the sigmoid and LinearModule::propagate_relevance() into the input x. No new rule is needed at the seam: the bridge composes the Datalog rule with LinearModule's epsilon rule (see LRP).

Relevance is conserved end to end: the other base facts' relevance plus the relevance reaching x sums to the seed.

Recipe: Datalog LRP bridge.
